title: Literal and metacharacter basics — Regular Expression Search
description: A regex is a pattern where most characters match themselves and metacharacters like . * + ? carry special meaning. Escaping with a backslash turns a metacharacter back into a literal, so '\.' matches a real period. Knowing exactly which characters are special in the engine at hand prevents the most common pattern bugs.
demo:
# Regex search: compile the pattern once, scan each line, report matches with spans.
import re
text = """see archive.txt and archive_txt here"""
pattern = r"archive\.txt"
rx = re.compile(pattern)
print("Pattern:", pattern)
found = False
for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
    for m in rx.finditer(line):
        found = True
        print(f"line {i} [{m.start()}:{m.end()}]: {m.group(0)!r}")
if not found:
    print("no matches")
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Character classes — Regular Expression Search
description: Bracket expressions like [0-9] or [a-zA-Z] match any single character from the listed set. Negated classes [^0-9] match anything outside the set, and shorthands like \d, \w, \s cover the everyday cases. Classes keep patterns readable where alternations of single characters would sprawl.

title: Quantifiers: greedy and lazy — Regular Expression Search
description: Quantifiers *, +, ?, and {m,n} repeat the preceding atom; by default they are greedy, consuming as much as possible. Appending ? makes them lazy, matching as little as possible, which changes what '<.*>' captures in '<a><b>'. Choosing greedy versus lazy correctly is the difference between one big match and many small ones.
demo: # Regex search: compile the pattern once, scan each line, report matches with spans. import re text = """one two""" pattern = r"<.*?>" rx = re.compile(pattern) print("Pattern:", pattern) found = False for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1): for m in rx.finditer(line): found = True print(f"line {i} [{m.start()}:{m.end()}]: {m.group(0)!r}") if not found: print("no matches")

title: Anchors and boundaries — Regular Expression Search
description: The anchors ^ and $ pin a match to the start or end of the string (or line, in multiline mode). The word boundary \b sits between word and non-word characters, so '\bcat\b' skips 'catalog'. Anchors turn substring search into whole-field validation, the basis of input checking.

title: Groups and capturing — Regular Expression Search
description: Parentheses group atoms for quantification and alternation, and by default they also capture the matched text. Numbered backreferences \1, \2 reuse a captured group later in the same pattern, enabling duplicate-word detection. Non-capturing groups (?:...) give the grouping without the bookkeeping overhead.

title: Alternation — Regular Expression Search
description: The pipe a|b tries the left branch first and falls back to the right, scoped by the enclosing group. Ordering matters: 'cat|catalog' on 'catalog' matches just 'cat' unless the longer branch comes first or a boundary is added. Alternation is how patterns express synonyms and spelling variants in one pass.

title: Backreferences and lookarounds — Regular Expression Search
description: Lookahead (?=...) and lookbehind (?<=...) assert context without consuming characters, so '\w+(?=:) ' finds labels. Negative variants (?!...) and (?<!...) assert absence, the regex way of saying 'not followed by'. These zero-width assertions add boolean-style conditions to otherwise linear patterns.

title: NFA simulation and backtracking — Regular Expression Search
description: Most popular engines implement regexes as nondeterministic finite automata explored with backtracking. Backtracking tries one path, and on failure rewinds to the last choice point to try another, which is why nested quantifiers like '(a+)+$' can explode exponentially. Understanding backtracking explains catastrophic slowdowns and motivates possessive quantifiers and atomic groups.

title: DFA-based matching — Regular Expression Search
description: DFA engines convert the pattern to a deterministic automaton once, then scan the text in guaranteed linear time. They give up backreferences and lookarounds but never suffer catastrophic backtracking. For untrusted patterns or huge inputs, linear-time engines are the safe choice.

title: Regex over large archives — Regular Expression Search
description: Scanning terabytes with one regex is I/O-bound, so engines split work across chunks and stream matches without loading whole files. Pre-filters like trigram indexes skip chunks that cannot match, running the full regex only on candidates. This two-phase design is how code search tools stay fast over entire repositories.

title: Multiline and dotall modes — Regular Expression Search
description: By default ^ and $ anchor to the whole string and . skips newlines; multiline mode makes anchors per-line and dotall lets . cross lines. Flags (or inline (?m), (?s)) switch these behaviors without rewriting the pattern. Choosing the right mode is essential when patterns span log entries or document sections.

title: Unicode character properties — Regular Expression Search
description: Modern engines match by Unicode property, so '\p{L}+' finds letters in any script, not just ASCII. Case-insensitive matching then follows Unicode case folding rules rather than ASCII upper/lower tables. Property-based patterns keep multilingual archives searchable with a single expression.

title: Replacement with regex — Regular Expression Search
description: Substitution replaces each match with a template that can reference captured groups, as in re.sub(r'(\w+)@(\w+)', r'\2/\1'). A replacement function can compute the substitute per match, enabling normalization and redaction pipelines. Regex replacement is the engine inside most text-cleaning workflows.

title: From regex to index-assisted search — Regular Expression Search
description: Trigram indexes extract all 3-character substrings of both the corpus and the pattern's required literals. Chunks lacking a required trigram are skipped without running the regex at all. This is how indexed code search answers regex queries over millions of files in under a second.
